summary: Discovery POC scoping with Crescent HealthTech focused on validating OpenAI-compatible endpoints and SDK-based integration for an EHR summarization + triage pilot. Key success criteria are latency (p95 < 450ms for short summaries), throughput support for 200 QPS peak with bursts to 600, and <3% hallucination rate on a clinical test set. Action items defined for SOW, benchmark harness, dataset, and security contacts. Plan to run first benchmarks in the first full week of April and reconvene after results.
transcript:
Header:
Date: 2027-03-22 16:00 PT
Duration: 54 minutes
Attendees: Sophie Morales (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Daniel Park (CTO, Crescent), Anika Shah (Lead ML Eng), Markus Le (PM)

Auto-summary (auto-gen, may be noisy): POC scoping call to map integration, success criteria: latency, throughput, hallucination thresholds; discuss OpenAI-compat SDK and function calling for EHR connector; plan benchmarks and timeline.

00:00 Sophie Morales: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh we'll kick off, I'm Sophie AE on the account, with Ravi our SE. Quick agenda — align on success criteria, workload, and the integration path (SDKs / openai-style endpoints / function calling).
00:18 Daniel Park: Thanks Sophie. From Crescent's side, I'm Daniel, CTO, and we want to validate a pilot that summarizes patient visit notes and surfaces triage flags. HIPAA obviously critical. We want to know if Redwood can do OpenAI-compat endpoints and also the function/tool calling for our EHR connector.
00:35 Sophie Morales: Yep, totally. Redwood supports an OpenAI-compatible adapter layer for simple lift-and-shift, and we also have SDKs for native integrations. Ravi, do you want to add detail on the function-calling shape?
00:44 Ravi Patel: Sure. So, the SDK will let you call model.generate or chat completions similarly to OpenAI patterns, plus we support a structured function calling interface. You can register a schema for the EHR actions, e.g., create_flag(patient_id, severity, code) and the runtime emits a structured payload. Note there are some differences in how we handle KV cache — sometimes transcribed as K-V cash — but it preserves the context for streaming.
01:10 Anika Shah: Quick Q — for function calling, do we need to change our data model? We want strongly typed output for downstream automation.
01:18 Ravi Patel: You can supply a JSON schema for the function signature and Redwood's OpenAI-compat layer will map the model output to that schema. For the POC we recommend starting with a narrow set of functions: summarize_visit, extract_medications, triage_flag. Keep responses small to hit latency SLOs.
01:38 Markus Le: Our product team cares about latency — we aim for sub-500ms p95 for short summaries seen by clinicians. Is that realistic on hosted?
01:46 Sophie Morales: Good question. Realistically, sub-500ms is tight for generation unless prompts and summary length are short. On hosted we can often hit 300–700ms for single-turn short outputs (<=150 tokens) on our smaller models. Dedicated or private deployments improve consistency and reduce tail latency. We should profile with your actual prompt patterns.
02:12 Daniel Park: We will provide sample traffic. For sizing, current traffic is 120 qps average, peaks up to 450 for surge windows. Could you handle that?
02:21 Ravi Patel: 120 qps sustained is doable. The key is batching and concurrency. We will model with a target of 200 qps steady state and burst to 600 for headroom. For the benchmark harness we'll simulate your qps and token distributions.
02:43 Anika Shah: About hallucination — we need measurables. What metric do you track?
02:49 Sophie Morales: We recommend a task-specific evaluation set and a defined acceptance threshold. For clinical summarization, historically customers set <3–5% critical hallucination on the test set. We'll add hallucination detection anchors to the evaluation harness.
03:05 Markus Le: On the security/compliance side, we need SOC2 plus HIPAA alignment, KMS integration, audit logs for every inference. Can Redwood provide that for a POC?
03:15 Sophie Morales: Yes — our Private deployment option supports customer-managed KMS and audit logs. For hosted POC we can enable enhanced logging and a SOC2 summary; full HIPAA program usually requires private or dedicated with contractual addendum. We'll send the security packet.
03:34 Daniel Park: What's the recommended integration path? We don't want to rewrite existing OpenAI calls across our stack.
03:40 Ravi Patel: Two options: 1) Adapter approach — use Redwood's OpenAI-compatible API endpoint (minimal code change), 2) SDK approach — use Redwood SDK for better observability (structured tracing, token-level costs, direct function registration). For POC we often recommend starting with the OpenAI-compat endpoint for speed, and then shift to SDK if you need more control.
04:05 Anika Shah: If we start with OpenAI-compat, can we still use function calling and structured output?
04:10 Ravi Patel: Yes, our compatibility layer supports the standard function calling JSON pattern. There are subtle differences in the shape of streaming chunks — we'll include a sample mapping.
04:22 Markus Le: Benchmarks — what do we need to provide?
04:25 Sophie Morales: Provide sample prompts, expected output length, dataset of ~1k representative records (de-identified) or synthetic analogs, traffic profile (qps, tokens per request, time-of-day), and acceptance criteria. We'll run a baseline on host and optionally a dedicated node to compare.
04:47 Daniel Park: We'd like comparison to OpenAI baseline as well — cost and latency.
04:52 Sophie Morales: We can run head-to-head on equivalent models and provide token-level cost estimates. Note that some model variants and quantization profiles differ — we'll document differences.
05:05 Anika Shah: For the structured output schema, we need discrete fields: problem_list, meds, allergies, triage_risk (low/med/high), and confidence scores. Can Redwood enforce schema and reject unparsable outputs?
05:20 Ravi Patel: The function-calling path enforces schema at inference mapping. If the model returns something that doesn't validate, the runtime flags it. You can configure strict-mode to cause a fall back to re-prompt or to return a structured error.
05:36 Markus Le: How about end-to-end latency when calling our EHR connector (we'll call an internal microservice after model output)? Any estimates?
05:45 Ravi Patel: Additive, so model latency + network to your service. For hosted, typical extra hop is ~40–80ms. With dedicated/private and colocated VPC peering, you can reduce that to <20ms. We'll factor that into end-to-end SLOs.
06:03 Daniel Park: We need to validate on PHI — can the POC run on private infra?
06:09 Sophie Morales: Yes, private deployment is possible but takes longer to provision. For POC we sometimes do a hybrid: run benchmark on hosted with de-identified data, sign a data processing addendum, then move validated workloads to Private for live PHI.
06:29 Anika Shah: About SDKs — language support? Node, Python?
06:33 Ravi Patel: Official SDKs: Python, Node, and a thin Go client. They expose both OpenAI-style endpoints and native calls for streaming, function registration, and trace metadata. We'll attach example repos.
06:52 Markus Le: On timelines, we want a 4-week POC: week 1 instrument + dataset, week 2 benchmark runs, week 3 iterate model/config, week 4 evaluation + decision. Is that feasible?
07:05 Sophie Morales: That's aggressive but feasible if the dataset is ready and compliance review doesn't block. We'll draft SOW with milestone gates and contingencies for Private infra provisioning.
07:20 Daniel Park: For benchmarks, what metrics will you produce?
07:24 Ravi Patel: We'll produce p50/p95/p99 latency, throughput, tokens/sec, cost per 1k tokens, hallucination rate on test set, structured output schema validation rate, and error/fallback rates. We'll also include memory/KV cache hit rates for performance tuning.
07:45 Anika Shah: One practical— do you support streaming partial summaries for UI while the final completes?
07:51 Ravi Patel: Yes, streaming is supported. It's compatible with our OpenAI-compat endpoint and SDK. It streams chunks and includes partial function payloads for longer jobs. Some clients may need to stitch chunks.
08:05 Markus Le: Any gotchas with rate limits during benchmark runs?
08:09 Sophie Morales: We'll provide a temporary higher quota for the POC. For sustained production quotas we size in Dedicated.
08:18 Daniel Park: For the benchmark harness — can you share a template?
08:21 Ravi Patel: Yes. We'll share a JMeter-like harness plus a python runner that hits the SDK and OpenAI-compat endpoints, collects timings, and validates structured outputs. We'll include basic load generators.
08:35 Anika Shah: Great. On cost — our procurement will evaluate per-token and reserved capacity. What rough numbers should we expect?
08:43 Sophie Morales: We'll include both per-token hosted pricing and an estimated reserved capacity monthly for your QPS profile. The SOW will contain a cost model for both short POC run and projected monthly cost at scale.
08:56 Markus Le: Regarding latency tuning — you mentioned batching and quantization. Are those automatic or manual?
09:03 Ravi Patel: A mix. Smart routing and autoscaling are automated; quantization profiles and kernel selection are recommended by our Optimize tooling and the runtime uses the best kernels but quantization requires explicit model variant selection per workload. We'll recommend configs in the SOW.
09:27 Daniel Park: We also use a third-party clinical QA tool. Can Redwood integrate to send structured outputs to that tool?
09:34 Ravi Patel: Yes, via our function calling you can push structured events to any downstream webhook or service, or use our built-in connectors. For the POC we'll prototype an EHR microservice call.
09:50 Anika Shah: Sample dataset — we'll sanitize 1k records and also provide a synthetic set. Any recommended format?
09:56 Sophie Morales: JSONL with fields: prompt, expected_summary, tokens_estimate, patient_age_bucket. For structured schema validation include expected key-value pairs.
10:08 Markus Le: Who will own the benchmark run on Redwood side?
10:11 Sophie Morales: Ravi will lead execution and I'll handle SOW and procurement coordination.
10:18 Daniel Park: Good. Any dependencies from our side?
10:21 Ravi Patel: Provide dataset, traffic profile, a test endpoint for EHR microservice or a stub, and compliance contact for NDA.
10:30 Anika Shah: If we hit errors in structured mapping, can we iterate model prompts programmatically?
10:35 Ravi Patel: Yes, the harness supports automated re-prompt loops in strict-mode to try a second pass before marking failure.
10:44 Markus Le: For acceptance: what is the exact gating?
10:49 Sophie Morales: We'll author acceptance tests: p95 latency < 450ms on short tasks, structured schema pass rate >= 98%, hallucination <= 3% on critical items, and throughput support for 200 qps steady. We'll include these in the SOW as pass/fail.
11:12 Daniel Park: Sounds good. Let's recap next steps.
11:15 Sophie Morales: Recap: Sophie sends draft SOW and pricing by 3/25; Ravi shares SDK guide, sample harness, and benchmark schedule by 3/28; Crescent provides dataset and traffic profile by 3/26; security packet to be shared by Redwood by 3/26; schedule first benchmark week of 4/4.
11:36 Markus Le: We'll review and revert on the SOW and compliance. Thanks team.
11:41 Sophie Morales: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up in email with materials and a calendar invite for the benchmark slot.
11:48 Daniel Park: Thanks. Bye.

End of call.

Notes: occasional transcription errors in product names ("Redood"), acronyms sometimes mistranscribed (KMS as K-M-S), filler words and short crosstalk present.

Explicit next steps recorded at end of transcript: Sophie to send SOW (3/25); Ravi to send harness + SDK (3/28); Crescent to provide dataset + profile (3/26); Security docs (3/26); Benchmark run in week of 4/4.
